faqs.q: What lip product formats does Lip Boxes make custom packaging for?
faqs.a: Folding cartons for lip balm, lipstick and lip gloss, rolled paperboard lip balm tubes, wrap labels, hang tab packs, rigid gift boxes and lip mask cartons, plus bulk programs that cover a whole range. All of them are quoted from a single inquiry.

faqs.q: What must be approved before custom lip packaging goes to print?

faqs.q: Which finishes can Lip Boxes apply to lip product cartons?
faqs.a: Soft-touch lamination, foil stamping, spot UV, holographic board and embossing are all available. Each is specified against your board and product rather than sold as a bundle, as set out in the coating and finish options for lip cartons.

faqs.q: What quality checks run on custom lip boxes before they ship?
faqs.a: Color is checked against the approved proof, dimensions are measured on the first sheets, and finished cartons go through a glue and fold test. Only then are they packed to your case count and released with tracking.

faqs.q: Can Lip Boxes package a range of several lip shades together?
faqs.a: Yes. Several shades or scents can share one die line, one board and one finish, with only the printed panel changing. That lets the designs share press sheets, which is usually the biggest saving on a multi-product lip launch.

faqs.q: Does Lip Boxes make packaging for lip masks and lip patches?

faqs.q: Do custom lip packaging orders ship ready-made from stock?
faqs.a: No. Nothing is held in stock, because every item is made to a die line drawn for a specific container. Each order moves through quoting, die line and proof approval, then production, so plan your schedule around those stages.

faqs.q: How are finished lip packaging orders packed and delivered?

/blog/how-packaging-quantity-affects-uni.h2: Questions on packaging quantity and unit pricing

faqs.q: Why does a larger packaging order cost so much less per unit?
faqs.a: A packaging quote combines once-per-job costs, such as the die, plates, make-ready and proofing, with per-unit costs like board and ink. Spread over a small run the setup dominates the price; spread over a large one it almost disappears.

faqs.q: Which packaging costs stay fixed regardless of the order quantity?
faqs.a: The die, the printing plates, press make-ready, any foil or emboss tooling and the proofing cycle all happen once per job. None of them change whether you order a short run or a very large one.

faqs.q: Which per-unit packaging costs fall only slowly as quantity rises?
faqs.a: Board, ink, laminate, press time for each sheet and any hand work are paid on every unit. They fall much more gently with volume than setup costs do, mostly through better material purchasing on larger runs.

faqs.q: Where is the biggest saving on the packaging quantity price curve?
faqs.a: At the start. Moving up from a very small run roughly halves the setup contribution and is often the largest proportional saving available, while pushing an already large packaging order higher changes the unit price very little.

faqs.q: Is ordering far more packaging always worth it for a lower unit price?
faqs.a: Not once you are ordering in the tens of thousands. Setup has already been absorbed at that point, so pushing volume further mostly moves cash into inventory rather than saving meaningful money on each carton.

faqs.q: How does print process choice change packaging unit prices on short runs?
faqs.a: Digital printing has no plate charge, so its cost curve is much flatter on short runs. Above roughly two thousand units, offset litho's lower per-unit cost takes over, and a quote for both shows where your job sits.

faqs.q: Why are foil and embossing so expensive on small packaging orders?
faqs.a: They add a fixed cost for the tooling and a per-unit cost for the extra pass. That double charge makes them disproportionately expensive at low volumes and far more reasonable once the tooling is spread across a large run.

faqs.q: How does standardizing a lip product range lower packaging unit prices?
faqs.a: When several products share one board, one ink set and one finish, they can be ganged onto shared press sheets and split the make-ready. On a multi-SKU launch that is frequently the biggest saving on the table.

faqs.q: Do packaging reorders carry the original die and proofing charges?
faqs.a: No. Once a die is cut and a proof approved, a repeat order carries no die or proofing charge. Mention a planned reorder cycle at quoting stage, as explained in how reorders and approvals work.

faqs.q: How should I read a published pack price on packaging?
faqs.a: As the price for that exact pack and specification. Ours is 100 boxes for $30.00 ($0.30 each) with free shipping; at larger quantities or a different specification, ask for pricing at your own quantity and at the next volume break.

/blog/how-to-choose-packaging-for-a-lip-.h2: Questions on choosing lip gloss line packaging

faqs.q: Why should the lip gloss tube be chosen before its carton?
faqs.a: A gloss tube is mostly applicator, so a small change in fill size can still change the carton height. Lock the primary container first, because its capped height drives the carton, the shipper, the case count and the pallet quantity.

faqs.q: Should I get lip gloss cartons quoted against two candidate tubes?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are still choosing between them. The cost difference is usually small, and it shows which tube is cheaper to package, a real factor that often gets ignored at the sampling stage of a gloss launch.

faqs.q: How does the shade count affect printing for a lip gloss line?
faqs.a: Shade count changes which print process makes sense more than total volume does. Digital has no plate charge per design, while offset litho charges plates per design unless shades are ganged, so give suppliers both the shade count and per-shade quantity.

faqs.q: What are the ways to show lip gloss color on the carton?
faqs.a: A die-cut window with a clear film patch shows the actual product, a spot Pantone swatch reproduces identically on every run, and a photographic swatch conveys finish as well as color. The three cost very different amounts.

faqs.q: Why can a photographic swatch drift on lip gloss cartons?
faqs.a: A photographic swatch on a model or an applicator smear is printed in process color, which varies slightly between runs. It conveys finish well, but it drifts between print runs of a gloss carton unless it is carefully managed.

faqs.q: Does kraft board suit a lip gloss line with many shades?
faqs.a: Usually not. Kraft mutes everything and will flatten the visible differences between several similar shades. Coated white board carries saturated color and fine gradients far better, which matters when gloss is bought on color.

faqs.q: Which board weight suits a single slim lip gloss carton?
faqs.a: Weight follows the pack rather than the look: around 16pt to 18pt for a single slim tube, and 22pt or more for duos and glass tubes. A tall gloss carton in light board bows visibly on a shelf.

faqs.q: Which coating gives a lip gloss carton a premium look affordably?
faqs.a: Matte lamination with spot UV on the swatch is the most reliable premium combination at a mid-market price. Choose it after the board, as the comparison of gloss carton coatings explains.

faqs.q: Why include inserts and shippers in the first lip gloss packaging quote?
faqs.a: Inserts for glass, window film, a leaflet for a long ingredient list and a shipper are each modest, yet together they can add more than the laminate did. They are far cheaper to include in the first quote than to add after tooling.

faqs.q: In what order should lip gloss packaging decisions be made?
faqs.a: Lock the tube, confirm shade count and per-shade quantity, choose how the shade is shown, pick the board, then the coating and any foil or spot UV. Add the forgotten extras, approve the die line, then proof each shade.

/blog/how-to-prepare-artwork-for-custom-.h2: Questions on preparing lip box artwork

faqs.q: Why should lip box artwork be built on the supplied die line?
faqs.a: The die line maps exactly where each cut and crease falls on the flat sheet. Designing to your own rectangle and hoping it fits the die is the most common cause of rework, so keep the die line on its own locked layer.

faqs.q: Should fonts be outlined in custom lip box artwork files?
faqs.a: Yes, or supplied alongside the file. Missing fonts substitute silently, and the substitution is not always obvious on a proof, so outlining text before you send lip box artwork removes that risk entirely.

faqs.q: Which color space should custom lip box artwork use?
faqs.a: Use CMYK for process work, plus named spot colors from the Pantone solid coated or uncoated library, whichever suits the stock. Spot colors are best kept for brand colors and shade swatches that must match exactly across every lip box run.

faqs.q: What regulated copy does a lip box sold in the US need?
faqs.a: A cosmetic sold in the United States needs an ingredient declaration in descending order of predominance, the net quantity of contents, and the name and place of business of the responsible party. Have that copy reviewed before approving the proof.

faqs.q: Why is small type harder to read on uncoated kraft lip boxes?
faqs.a: Ink spreads into the fiber of uncoated kraft, so fine type loses definition sooner than it does on coated board. Legibility already falls off sharply below about 5 pt, and kraft pushes that limit higher still.

faqs.q: What quick checks catch most lip box artwork problems before sending?
faqs.a: Confirm the die line layer is present and unmoved, bleed passes every trim edge, the separations show only the plates you intended, the barcode sits on a flat panel off any crease, and the smallest type reads at full size.

faqs.q: Why check the separations before sending lip box print files?
faqs.a: The separations preview shows every plate your file will produce. Stray spot colors carried in from placed artwork become extra plates, so confirm you have exactly the plates you intended before submitting the lip box files.

faqs.q: Why is approving an outdated file a risk on multi-SKU lip ranges?
faqs.a: On a range with many shades, approving an outdated file is a more common failure than any production error. Naming every file with the product, the die line reference and a revision number keeps the right version in front of the approver.

faqs.q: Why can artwork crossing a paper lip balm tube seam show a step?
faqs.a: A rolled tube template is a rectangle whose width is the circumference plus a seam overlap. Where artwork crosses that overlap the two edges meet slightly offset, so keep critical graphics and text away from the tube seam.

faqs.q: Should lip box artwork stop exactly at the trim line?
faqs.a: No. Artwork should continue into the bleed beyond every trimmed edge rather than stopping at the trim, so a slight cutting variation never leaves a white sliver showing along the edge of the finished lip box.

/blog/lip-balm-box-materials-compared/.h2: Questions on lip balm box board grades

faqs.q: What are the four board families used for lip balm boxes?
faqs.a: Coated white SBS folding boxboard, unbleached kraft board, recycled board with a white printing face, and rigid board with a printed wrap. The last is a different construction entirely and belongs to gift packaging rather than everyday retail cartons.

faqs.q: Why is SBS board the default for full-color lip balm cartons?
faqs.a: It is bleached, coated on the print side and bright white beneath the ink, so colors reproduce close to their intended values. Small type and fine halftones also hold well on it, which suits detailed cosmetic artwork.

faqs.q: Can kraft lip balm boxes print a true white?
faqs.a: Not on their own. Kraft is unbleached, uncoated and brown, so it prints warm and dark. Anything on a kraft lip balm box that must read as white needs an opaque white underprint laid down first.

faqs.q: Which lip balm box board grade is actually the strongest?
faqs.a: In practice weight dominates, not grade. An 18pt SBS carton and an 18pt kraft carton behave similarly under load, while a 14pt carton in either grade will feel flimsy once it is sitting on a shelf.

faqs.q: What board weight suits a tall or multi-tube lip balm carton?
faqs.a: For a carton over three inches tall, or one holding more than one tube, move up to 20pt or 24pt board. A counter display holding a dozen sticks should be E-flute corrugated rather than any paperboard.

faqs.q: How much does board choice affect lip balm box cost?
faqs.a: Less than most people assume, especially at low volumes where setup dominates. Recycled board is the cheapest per sheet, SBS sits in the middle and kraft is comparable or slightly higher, while rigid construction is a different bracket.

faqs.q: Can the board choice remove a production pass on lip balm boxes?
faqs.a: Yes, and that often matters more than the board price. A design that works on kraft with two spot colors and a varnish costs less than the same design on SBS with four-color process and a laminate.

faqs.q: Which board grade suits a natural or unbleached lip balm brand?
faqs.a: Kraft, provided you accept that color will print muted. If the range instead depends on shoppers telling bright colors apart at arm's length, coated SBS is the better choice for the lip balm carton.

faqs.q: When does rigid construction make sense for lip balm packaging?
faqs.a: When the pack is a gift and the opening moment is part of what you are selling. Expect a different price bracket, since rigid board, a printed wrap and hand assembly cost far more than any folding carton.

faqs.q: Why ask for a printed proof on the actual lip balm box board?
faqs.a: Board is the one variable a screen proof cannot represent. The same artwork prints genuinely differently on SBS, kraft, recycled and wrapped rigid stock, so approve the color on the board you will actually use.

/blog/lipstick-packaging-sizes-and-struc.h2: Questions on lipstick box sizes and structures

faqs.q: What size range do single lipstick bullet cartons usually fall into?
faqs.a: For orientation only, a single-bullet carton commonly falls between 0.9 and 1.2 inches square and 3 to 3.5 inches tall. Treat that as the range you will land in, not as a size to order.

faqs.q: Which three measurements should I take on a lipstick case?
faqs.a: Width at the widest point with the cap fitted, depth at that same point since square and oval cases differ on the two axes, and total height with the cap fully seated rather than the barrel alone.

faqs.q: Where is the widest point on a tapered lipstick case?
faqs.a: On many lipstick cases the widest point is the cap itself, but on tapered cases it sits lower down the barrel. Measure along the full length with the cap fitted and use the largest width you find.

faqs.q: Why can a lacquered lipstick case bind inside its carton?
faqs.a: The lacquer coating can make the case marginally larger than its bare-metal specification. A carton built to the nominal drawing then binds on every unit, which is why a measured sample beats a supplier drawing.

faqs.q: What if I can only send a drawing of my lipstick case?
faqs.a: Send the drawing and say explicitly that it is a drawing rather than a measured sample. That lets extra clearance be allowed in the carton, since supplier drawings frequently omit real-world tolerances.

faqs.q: Why do lipstick duos and trios need a partition?
faqs.a: Lacquered and foiled cases scratch each other when they move together inside a carton. For sets a partition is not optional, because a lipstick set that arrives marked defeats the whole point of the pack.

faqs.q: Which lipstick carton closure keeps the front panel uninterrupted?
faqs.a: A straight tuck end, where both flaps tuck from the same side, keeps the front panel clear for artwork. A reverse tuck costs the same but closes from opposite ends, and a seal end is glued shut on the filling line.

faqs.q: How much clear width does a barcode need on a lipstick carton?
faqs.a: About 1.5 inches of clear width on a flat panel away from creases. On a slim lipstick carton that competes with shade name, net weight, ingredients and responsible party details, so allocate the panels before designing.

faqs.q: When does a lipstick presentation tray belong in a rigid box?
faqs.a: When the opening moment is part of the product. A fitted tray that presents the bullet at an angle suits rigid lipstick boxes with fitted trays rather than a folding carton.

faqs.q: Is a sleeve and tray a good structure for lipstick packaging?
faqs.a: It can be, where presence matters. A sleeve and tray is two pieces, so it costs more than a tuck carton but gives a more considered opening, which suits gift sets and higher price points better than everyday retail.

/blog/packaging-inserts-for-lipstick-and.h2: Questions on lipstick and lip gloss inserts

faqs.q: What two jobs does a lipstick or lip gloss insert do?
faqs.a: Restraint, which stops the product moving inside the carton, and presentation, which controls what the customer sees when the box opens. Restraint is the job that costs you money when it is missing.

faqs.q: What damage happens when a lipstick moves inside its carton?
faqs.a: A lipstick case is dense for its size and slides under its own inertia. Repeated movement marks the case finish and scuffs the printed interior, so the customer receives something that looks like returned stock.

faqs.q: When does an insert stop being optional for lip product packaging?
faqs.a: When the carton holds more than one item, the product is glass, the case finish marks easily, the carton has generous clearance for hand packing, the pack ships direct to consumers, or the opening moment is part of the sale.

faqs.q: Why do glass lip gloss tubes chip inside tall cartons?
faqs.a: Glass chips at the neck when it slides inside a tall carton during handling. An insert that holds the tube still prevents that, which is why glass is one of the cases where a gloss insert is not optional.

faqs.q: Why do soft-touch or foiled lipstick cases need an insert?
faqs.a: Lacquered, foiled and soft-touch finishes mark easily, and a loose case rubbing against the carton wall in transit will show it. Restraining the case protects the finish the customer is paying for.

faqs.q: What does an insert add to a rigid lipstick gift box?
faqs.a: In a rigid box the insert does proportionally more work, because the format is about the moment the lid lifts. A tray presenting the bullet at a slight angle, in a contrasting recess, communicates the brand as much as it protects.

faqs.q: Do satin or velvet trays complicate lip gift box disposal?
faqs.a: Yes. Satin, velvet and flocked trays give the deepest luxury read, but they add components that will not recycle with the board, so the customer has more than one material to deal with when the box is discarded.

faqs.q: What alternative to a velvet lipstick tray still looks luxurious?
faqs.a: A die-cut card platform in a contrasting printed paper achieves much of the same effect while keeping the pack closer to a single material stream. It suits rigid lipstick and gloss boxes where presentation matters.

faqs.q: Why does generous carton clearance call for a lip product insert?
faqs.a: Cartons sized with extra room for a hand-packing line let the product shift in transit. An insert takes up that space so the lipstick or gloss stays put and arrives looking as new as it left the filling line.

faqs.q: Does a multi-item lipstick or gloss set always need an insert?
faqs.a: Yes. When a carton holds more than one item, the products can knock against each other in transit, so an insert or partition is needed to keep each lipstick or gloss separated and unmarked.

/blog/paper-lip-balm-tubes-and-their-pac.h2: Questions on paper lip balm tubes

faqs.q: What is a paper lip balm tube actually made of?
faqs.a: A rolled multi-ply paperboard cylinder with a friction-fit cap and a disc in the base that pushes the product upward. There is no threaded plastic mechanism, which is the main reason brands choose the format.

faqs.q: What does the inner liner do in a paper lip balm tube?
faqs.a: It sits between the balm and the board and stops oil migrating into the paper. With the wrong liner grade the tube darkens at the edges within weeks, which looks like a defect even though the tube is structurally fine.

faqs.q: Which balm formulas suit paper lip balm tubes best?
faqs.a: Higher wax ratio formulas hold up considerably better, and a firm beeswax and butter balm is well suited. Formulas high in liquid oils need a heavier barrier liner, and balms that stay soft at room temperature are a poor fit.

faqs.q: How are paper lip balm tubes filled on a production line?
faqs.a: From the top, with the base disc already seated, then left upright and undisturbed to cool. Most fillers settle on a pour temperature a few degrees above the set point of the balm.

faqs.q: Why does pour temperature matter when filling paper lip balm tubes?
faqs.a: Too hot and the balm wicks past the liner edge into the board; too cool and it sets before it levels. Getting the pour right protects both the appearance and the barrier of the paper tube.

faqs.q: How should I explain the push-up action of a paper lip balm tube?
faqs.a: Say on the pack or in the product description that the balm pushes up gently from the base and does not retract. A short line like that costs nothing and turns a perceived fault into an understood characteristic.

faqs.q: Can paper lip balm tubes be sold without a carton?
faqs.a: Yes. A paper tube prints directly and needs no label, so it can be sold bare, as with printed paper lip balm tubes. Many brands still add a slim carton for theft prevention, protection and legal copy.

faqs.q: Can a paper lip balm tube carton hang on a peg?
faqs.a: Yes. Where the pack goes onto a peg fixture, a hang tab is added to the slim carton around the tube. That carton can also carry the ingredient declaration that the tube's small circumference struggles to hold.

faqs.q: Why keep filled paper lip balm tubes away from summer heat?
faqs.a: Paper tubes are more heat-sensitive than plastic, and a pallet stored high under a hot roof in summer will show it. Keep filled stock cool, and treat storage after filling as part of the specification.

faqs.q: Is a paper lip balm tube liner recyclable with paper?
faqs.a: That depends. The liner is a coating, and whether a specific liner grade suits standard paper recycling varies by material and by municipality, so confirm the exact grade with your supplier before writing any claim on the pack.

/blog/printing-methods-for-cosmetic-pack.h2: Questions on printing methods for cosmetic packaging

faqs.q: Do all mainstream printing methods produce acceptable cosmetic cartons?
faqs.a: Yes. Digital, offset litho, flexo and screen all produce commercially acceptable cosmetic cartons. What separates them is where their costs sit and which substrates and color profiles each process suits best.

faqs.q: What is digital printing best suited to in cosmetic packaging?
faqs.a: Multiple designs, variable data and fast turnaround. With no plate charge its setup cost is close to zero and its unit cost stays roughly flat, which makes it the natural choice for short runs and wide shade ranges.

faqs.q: What is offset litho best suited to in cosmetic packaging?
faqs.a: Fine halftones, small type and the widest range of stocks, with a unit cost that falls steeply at volume. Plates are charged once per design, so offset litho pays off on larger cosmetic carton runs.

faqs.q: When does flexo printing suit cosmetic packaging?
faqs.a: Flexo suits uncoated kraft, simple spot-color work and labels. It is less suited to fine gradients and small reverse-out type, so it works best on bold, simple cosmetic packaging designs.

faqs.q: What is screen printing used for on cosmetic cartons?
faqs.a: Heavy opaque ink, such as a thick white on dark stock, applied at any quantity as an added pass. It captures photographic detail poorly and is slow as a primary process, so it is rarely used for a whole carton.

faqs.q: Why does four-color process drift on cosmetic shade swatches?
faqs.a: Process builds a color from cyan, magenta, yellow and black, and it drifts within normal tolerance between runs. That is invisible on a photograph but very visible on a flat brand color or a shade swatch.

faqs.q: Why use a spot Pantone ink on cosmetic packaging?
faqs.a: A spot Pantone is a pre-mixed ink that reproduces identically every time. It costs an extra ink station, but when a customer compares a nude swatch with one bought months ago, that consistency is worth paying for.

faqs.q: What ink setup do most cosmetic cartons end up using?
faqs.a: Process plus one or two spot colors: process for imagery, and spots for the brand color and the shade swatch. The printing options for lip packaging set out what each combination involves.

faqs.q: What three checks should I make on a cosmetic packaging proof?
faqs.a: Check that spot colors match their references under daylight rather than indoor lighting, that the smallest type is legible at final size, and that any shade swatch reads correctly next to the actual product.

faqs.q: Does black-through board change how cosmetic cartons print?

faqs.q: What is the difference between straight tuck and reverse tuck lip boxes?
faqs.a: On a straight tuck both flaps tuck from the same side, which keeps the front panel uninterrupted for artwork. A reverse tuck costs the same with flaps closing from opposite ends, and some fillers prefer it.

faqs.q: Why does the base matter most on a lip product carton?
faqs.a: The base is the part that fails. A carton that opens downward when someone lifts it by the top drops the product on the floor, so the base is chosen against the packed weight of the lip product.

faqs.q: Is an auto-bottom base worth it for hand-packed lip cartons?
faqs.a: Often. Auto-bottom cartons cost more per unit than a tuck base but form as they open, so they assemble faster. On a hand-packing operation running thousands of units, that frequently pays for itself in labor.

faqs.q: When does a lip product carton need a snap-lock base?
faqs.a: When it holds two items or is tall. A snap-lock base locks flat as the carton is opened and holds better than a simple tuck flap once the packed weight goes beyond a single light lip balm stick or gloss tube.

faqs.q: Do hang tab lip boxes need a separate plastic hook?
faqs.a: No. The tab is die-cut from the same board as the carton, so there is no separate hook to source or dispose of. Euro slot, round hole, delta cut and extended header shapes are covered on hang tab lip balm boxes.

faqs.q: Which rigid box style is the least expensive for lip products?
faqs.a: The two-piece lid and base. A separate lid lifts off a base, giving a sturdy, simple rigid box that costs less than the magnetic book, drawer and sleeve, or shoulder neck constructions.

faqs.q: What is a shoulder neck rigid box for lip products?
faqs.a: A rigid box where the lid and base are separated by a visible collar. That gap allows a contrasting color or material, adding a considered detail to lipstick, gloss and gift sets.

faqs.q: What display structures can be made alongside lip product cartons?
faqs.a: Counter display units, shelf-ready trays, clip strips and printed mailer boxes. These hold other packs rather than a product, serving checkout counters, store shelves, secondary placement and direct-to-consumer shipping.

faqs.q: Which four questions decide the right lip box style?
faqs.a: How the product is filled, how much the packed carton weighs, where it is merchandised and whether the opening is part of the product. Those answers point to the closure, the base, the tab and the construction.

faqs.q: What is a sleeve and tray lip box?
faqs.a: A printed band that slides over an inner tray. It has two components, so it costs more than a tuck carton, but it gives more presence and suits lip products where the opening is part of the experience.

faqs.a: The die line is drawn for your container, the board grade and weight are chosen for your pack, the print process suits your quantity and color count, and finishing is specified per job rather than bundled.

faqs.q: Why are there no bundled finishing packages on custom lip packaging?

faqs.q: What are the six stages of a custom lip packaging project?

faqs.q: What do I receive in a written custom lip packaging quote?

faqs.q: Which decisions drive the cost of custom lip packaging most?
faqs.a: Quantity, board grade and weight, color count, finishing passes, and structure and insert. Each is cheap to decide early and expensive to change after tooling, so settle them before the die is cut.

faqs.q: Why test a plain structural sample with real lip product inside?
faqs.a: A fit that works on paper can fail with a slightly pillowed sachet or a lacquered case that measures larger than specified. Testing with real product shows whether the carton fits, stands, closes and holds, as covered under structural sample options.

faqs.q: Why do lip products specified separately rarely look like a range?
faqs.a: Products specified one at a time over many months tend to end up on different boards, finishes and print processes. Fixing those once for the whole range keeps every pack consistent and lets designs share press sheets.

faqs.q: How little information do I need to start a custom lip packaging inquiry?
faqs.a: A sentence describing the product and a quantity is enough to open a conversation. The team will tell you what else is needed rather than expecting a full specification from you up front.

faqs.q: Does custom lip packaging allow an opaque white underprint?
faqs.a: Yes, where the chosen stock needs it. Color count covers process, spot colors and whether an opaque white underprint is required, which is common on kraft, metallized and holographic board.

faqs.q: Why is each custom lip packaging die line drawn from scratch?
faqs.a: Because no two containers are exactly alike. Each die line is drawn for your specific container rather than picked from a size chart or adjusted from another job, so the fit depends on your real measurements.

faqs.q: Which finish suits lip balm cartons sold from self-service pegs?
faqs.a: Laminate or a hard varnish, because bare digital print scuffs at the seams within weeks of being picked up and put back by shoppers. On a peg fixture the finish is about durability first and looks second.

faqs.q: Is a varnish enough for lip cartons shipped inside mailers?
faqs.a: Often, yes. In boxed e-commerce the carton is protected by its mailer, so a varnish usually gives enough surface protection without paying for lamination the lip carton does not need.

faqs.q: How does soft-touch lamination change a lip product carton?
faqs.a: It gives a velvety surface that is warm to the hand and reads premium, though it can mark on very dark solids. Soft-touch costs more than matte or gloss lamination on the same lip carton.

faqs.q: When is hot foil stamping most effective on lip boxes?
faqs.a: On logos and thin frames. Hot foil is real metal leaf pressed in with heat and pressure, genuinely reflective in a way metallic ink is not, but large solid foil areas are harder to lay down evenly.

faqs.q: Why choose spot UV instead of foil on a lip gloss carton?
faqs.a: Spot UV puts gloss varnish on selected artwork over a matte background, giving high contrast for a fraction of the cost of foil. It is the most economical way to suggest shine on a lip gloss carton.

faqs.q: Does embossing work on uncoated lip boxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Embossing and debossing need no ink and work on both coated and uncoated stock, though they hold far more definition on rigid board than on thin folding board used for lip cartons.

faqs.q: Which lip packaging finish is the cheapest option?
faqs.a: Varnish, by a clear margin, because it runs inline with printing. Lamination adds a converting pass and material, spot UV adds modest tooling, and foil or emboss add a metal die plus a pass.

faqs.q: Why does holographic board stay costly at higher lip box volumes?
faqs.a: It carries a material premium on every unit that does not fall away with volume the way tooling does. Foil and emboss, by contrast, become quite reasonable once their dies are spread across a large run.

faqs.q: Do extra finishes add production time to lip packaging?
faqs.a: Yes. Each additional pass adds production time, so with a fixed launch date say so at quoting stage. The lead times for lip packaging explain how finishing passes affect the schedule.

faqs.q: When do metallic or pearlescent inks suit lip packaging?
faqs.a: When you want shimmer across large areas that foil cannot economically cover. They are subtler than foil and considerably cheaper at scale, which suits lip gloss and balm cartons with wide printed areas.

faqs.a: Pennsylvania focuses on private label and pharmacy supply, where a cost target comes first and one carton structure is shared across brands. Texas also covers private label programs running several brand names from a single die line across five large metros.

faqs.q: Which state guide explains seasonal lip balm ordering and call-off delivery?
faqs.a: The Michigan guide. Winter concentrates lip balm demand into a few months, and the guide explains how a scheduled call-off produces the full quantity in one run at the volume price, then releases stock in stages as the season builds.

faqs.q: Do the state guides cover direct-to-consumer lip product mailers?
faqs.a: The Virginia guide covers direct-to-consumer fulfillment. It explains why a retail carton should never ship loose, what a printed mailer and insert add, how parcel rate bands affect cost, and the intake rules fulfillment centers enforce on deliveries.

faqs.q: Which state guide suits a lip brand selling into prestige department stores?
faqs.a: The New York guide. Prestige accounts issue packaging manuals covering dimensions, barcode placement, case counts and sometimes material restrictions, and the guide explains why that manual should reach us before the die line is approved rather than after.

faqs.q: Which paper tube liner grade suits lip balm kept in hot Arizona storage?
faqs.a: A softened balm can wick past a light liner edge in heat, so specify a heavier barrier grade if the product will sit in uncontrolled storage. Where a paper tube is chosen for positioning, a firmer wax ratio in the formula also matters more than usual in Arizona.

faqs.q: How should an Arizona receiving bay handle a delivery of lip balm labels?
faqs.a: If the receiving area is not climate controlled, ask for the consignment to be scheduled rather than left, and move label stock indoors promptly. Label rolls are the component most affected by sitting in a hot Arizona receiving bay, because adhesive softens and oozes at the edges.

faqs.q: Is a folding carton enough for California direct-to-consumer lip product orders?
faqs.a: No. A folding carton posted loose arrives crushed, so California brands selling direct to consumers usually pair the carton with a printed mailer. Flat cartons and labels pack densely, while assembled rigid boxes and paper tubes take far more space per unit.

faqs.q: Do Colorado specialty retailers expect a barcode on small-batch lip balm?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Small Colorado brands frequently forget a barcode until an independent store asks for one, so plan its position before artwork is finished. It needs a flat panel inside the safe area and should never cross a crease line on the carton or tube.

faqs.q: Which stocks suit Colorado apothecary and herbal lip care packaging?
faqs.a: Colorado apothecary and outdoor lip care tends toward unbleached and uncoated stocks with restrained printing, because independent buyers judge packs at close range and a pack that looks mass-produced can work against the brand. Plain kraft push-up tubes with a printed label suit small batches well.

faqs.q: Can a printed band turn two Florida resort singles into a gift set?
faqs.a: Yes. A printed band or belly wrap turns two existing singles into a set without a new carton die, which makes it the cheapest way to create a gift SKU for Florida resort, hotel and souvenir retail from stock you already hold.

faqs.q: Which finishes suit lip packaging sold in Florida tourism retail?
faqs.a: Florida resort and airport stores use bright lighting and attract impulse gift buyers, so finishes that read well under strong light help. Laminated cartons resist handling, holographic or metallized stock suits limited editions, and window cartons work where the shade itself is the selling point.

faqs.q: Should a Georgia gloss brand use holographic foil or full holographic board?
faqs.a: For a small Georgia gloss launch, holographic foil on the logo usually makes more sense, because full holographic board is a material premium on every unit. Foil still catches light and reads as movement on camera, which suits brands that sell mostly through images.

faqs.q: What should a Georgia brand shipping from home tell us when quoting?
faqs.a: Say at quoting stage that delivery is to a residence or small studio rather than a commercial address. Residential delivery changes the carrier service, and a pallet arriving at a Georgia house without a liftgate arranged is easier to prevent than fix.

faqs.q: Who should approve proofs for an Illinois mass retail reset order?
faqs.a: Nominate one person with authority to approve proofs. On Illinois reset work, approval time is more often the binding constraint than production time, and a proof circulating for consensus is the most common cause of missing a distribution center cutoff.

faqs.q: How does fixture depth limit a lip pack for Illinois chain retail?
faqs.a: The pack must clear the one hanging in front of it on the fixture, so fixture depth sets the maximum carton depth for Illinois chain accounts. Collect that figure, along with peg diameter and spacing, from the retailer before a die line is drawn.

faqs.q: Why does volume rather than weight decide how Indiana lip shipments pack?
faqs.a: Lip products are light, so a case fills up by volume long before it gets heavy. For Indiana distribution that makes units per case and per pallet the figures that decide how many cases each delivery and each onward shipment takes.

faqs.q: Should Indiana pallets be stretch wrapped, strapped or slip sheeted?
faqs.a: That depends on what your Indiana operation or your retail accounts require. Tell us the pallet finishing method with the inquiry, along with the case dimensions, maximum height and labeling rules, so the consignment is built to that specification from the start.

faqs.q: Why do Maryland promotional lip balm programs rely on labels over cartons?
faqs.a: A logo on a wrap label is faster and cheaper to change per client than a printed carton. For Maryland conference and corporate gifting work, one tube stock with one label size lets each new client become a label print rather than a full packaging project.

faqs.q: What matters most in packaging for Maryland conference giveaway lip balm?
faqs.a: Promotional packs are not sold, so there is no shelf to compete on. What matters for Maryland giveaways is that the recipient's organization is identifiable, the unit cost is predictable and the quantity arrives by the event date.

faqs.q: Why does a Massachusetts lip mask suit a carton with a window?
faqs.a: A lip mask is the one treatment format where a window helps, because the patch shape explains the product without any copy. For other Massachusetts treatment products, a window should be used only where showing the product genuinely informs the buyer.

faqs.q: Should directions and wear time get their own panel on Massachusetts treatment packs?
faqs.a: Yes. Treatment positioning needs directions and wear time given a dedicated panel rather than squeezed into a margin, with type set at a size people can actually read. Allowing that panel area is a sizing decision to settle before the container is chosen.

faqs.q: How should a Michigan hang tab be specified for a winter multipack?
faqs.a: The tab geometry has to be specified against the packed weight of the multipack rather than a single stick. A lot of Michigan winter lip balm sells from pharmacy and convenience checkout pegs, so a tab sized for one tube can tear under a heavier pack.

faqs.q: When should the last call-off release land for Michigan winter lip balm?
faqs.a: Set a cutoff for the final release so the last tranche is not still arriving in February, after most Michigan winter demand has passed. Tie the release schedule to when stock is actually needed rather than to even monthly intervals.

faqs.q: Why does a Missouri chain listing favor coated white board over kraft?
faqs.a: Kraft and recycled boards vary more between mill batches than coated white board. Across a dozen reorders spread over several years on a Missouri regional chain listing, that variation shows on the shelf, so coated white keeps the pack reproducing closer to the original.

faqs.q: Should Missouri brands specify a named laminate rather than a generic finish?
faqs.a: Yes. Name one laminate or varnish specification rather than writing a generic matte finish, because a generic description lets the finish change between reorders. On a long Missouri listing, that small drift adds up until the shelf pack no longer matches the one the buyer approved.

faqs.q: Will a New Jersey reviewer see the laid-out artwork before proof approval?
faqs.a: Yes. We print the approved file and do not review its regulatory content, but we make sure your New Jersey reviewer sees the laid-out artwork rather than only the copy in a document, because size and legibility only become clear once it is set.

faqs.q: What causes the most serious artwork error on New Jersey multi-SKU programs?
faqs.a: An outdated file being approved. On a New Jersey program with several SKUs in circulation, name every file with SKU code, die line reference and revision number, record approvals against a specific revision, and move superseded files out of the working folder.

faqs.q: Which finish combination signals prestige on New York department store lip packs?
faqs.a: Soft-touch lamination with a hot foil detail is the finish that most reliably signals prestige, because the two do different jobs. The laminate changes how the pack feels and the foil changes how it looks, which suits close-range judgment in New York prestige retail.

faqs.q: Do New York prestige accounts require testing before a first delivery?
faqs.a: Some do. Certain New York prestige account manuals specify a first-article or drop test before delivery, so read the full packaging manual at quoting stage and send it with your inquiry rather than meeting that clause when the goods are ready.

faqs.q: Why does machine erection change carton bases for North Carolina fillers?
faqs.a: Whether cartons are erected by hand or by machine changes the base construction, so a North Carolina contract filler should confirm this before the die line is drawn. A base suited to hand packing can be unusable on an automated line, however good the printing.

faqs.q: Which carton feed orientation should a North Carolina filling line specify?
faqs.a: Tell us the feed orientation the carton magazine on your North Carolina line expects, together with closure method and case count. Those details shape the die line, so they are cheap to build in at inquiry stage and expensive to change after approval.

faqs.q: Which base construction should an Ohio test market carton use?
faqs.a: Choose the base the rollout will need, such as an auto-bottom or seal end for an automated line, even if the Ohio trial is hand packed. Base construction is cheap to get right at trial stage and expensive to change once artwork is signed off.

faqs.q: Why should Ohio test market artwork use spot colors from the start?
faqs.a: Spot colors reproduce identically between runs, while a process build drifts within tolerance. Specifying spots on the Ohio trial means the rollout pack matches the one that was tested, so the results stay readable and the artwork carries forward unchanged.

faqs.q: Why should Pennsylvania private label brands avoid tweaking a shared carton?
faqs.a: A small dimensional change for one account creates a second die and breaks the shared economics. Pennsylvania private label programs work when the structure stays fixed and only artwork changes, so the die line, structural sample and fit testing are spread across every brand.

faqs.q: Which three choices move a Pennsylvania pharmacy carton price most?
faqs.a: Board weight, color count and whether the job carries any finishing pass account for most of the difference between one Pennsylvania pharmacy carton price and another. Starting from a cost target and building the specification inside it produces different answers from choosing a finish first.

faqs.q: Which pack shape sells best at a Tennessee merchandise table?
faqs.a: Tennessee tour and venue merchandise usually sells from a table rather than a fixture, so a pack that stacks and sits face-up works better than a tall slim carton. A flatter proportion or a multipack tray also survives a queue handling it and travel in a road case.

faqs.q: Why suit plain tubes with printed labels to Tennessee tour merchandise?
faqs.a: Tour quantities are modest and reorders are unpredictable. With a plain container and a printed label, more labels can be produced quickly against existing tube stock if a Tennessee product sells faster than expected, rather than waiting on a full printed container run.

faqs.q: How should Texas cases be labeled for split metro deliveries?
faqs.a: Case labeling should identify the SKU without anyone opening the case, and some Texas accounts require a specific barcode format on the outer case. Building those requirements into the production plan costs nothing, while relabeling finished stock later costs labor and risks damage.

faqs.q: Which Texas lip brands most often order salon and med-spa packaging?
faqs.a: Salon and med-spa retail lines concentrate in Dallas and Houston and tend to order modest quantities frequently rather than large quantities occasionally. Holding the die line and approved proof makes those Texas reorders simpler, since repeat orders carry no die or proofing charge.

faqs.q: Should Virginia online lip brands print the inside of a mailer?
faqs.a: Often it is worth it, since for an online Virginia brand the opening moment is the whole brand experience. Interior printing or a printed card inside a plain mailer both work, and a pack that opens without scissors features in a lot of customer feedback.

faqs.q: How do parcel rate bands affect Virginia lip product mailer sizing?
faqs.a: Dimensions that fit a standard parcel rate band can materially change shipping cost, and being fractionally over a threshold adds up on every order. Check the bands with your carrier before the Virginia mailer size is fixed, and keep weight down where the customer pays shipping.

faqs.q: Is metallized board accepted in Washington paper recycling streams?
faqs.a: No. Metallized board is not recyclable in a paper stream, and describing it otherwise is the kind of claim that gets a brand challenged by Washington buyers. Where disposal wording matters, uncoated or varnished stocks keep the pack closer to a single material stream.

faqs.q: Why do Washington lip brands prefer printed swatches over film windows?
faqs.a: A film window adds a second material the consumer must separate, while a printed swatch keeps the carton in the paper stream. The trade-off is that a Washington shopper cannot see the actual product so the printed swatch has to carry the color accurately.

/materials/.h2: Questions about lip packaging board materials

faqs.q: Which board grade suits full-color lipstick and lip balm cartons?
faqs.a: Bleached coated board, often called SBS, is the default for full-color cosmetic cartons. It reproduces closest to proof and holds fine halftones and small type, which matters when shoppers have to tell several lip shades apart at arm's length.

faqs.q: When does a lip packaging carton need black-through board?
faqs.a: Use black-through board when a carton is printed dark and white cut edges would show. Standard board is white in the middle, so every die-cut edge and crease shows a thin white line on a black soft-touch pack, which cannot be fixed after production.

faqs.q: What board weight suits a single lip balm stick carton?
faqs.a: A single lip balm stick, gloss tube or lipstick bullet needs only a light board, and that weight is the most common specification we quote, adjusted against packed weight. Send the weight of the packed carton rather than the empty one, since that figure decides board weight and base style.

faqs.q: Does a four-tube lip balm multipack need heavier board?
faqs.a: Yes. Multipacks, three-packs, glass primaries and hanging packs all need more board than the carton size suggests, and the heavier grades feel noticeably more substantial in the hand. A hanging pack may also need tab reinforcement, decided from the packed weight.

faqs.q: Why does kraft board change how lip packaging colors print?
faqs.a: Uncoated kraft is warmer and darker throughout and absorbs ink into the fiber, so every color reads warmer and there is no true white. Light colors need an opaque white layer printed underneath, which has to exist in the artwork as its own named layer.

faqs.q: What liner should a paper lip balm tube use for oily balms?
faqs.a: A standard grease-resistant liner handles firm beeswax and butter formulas. Balms high in liquid oils, or poured warm and left soft, need a heavier barrier grade. We confirm exactly which liner is quoted so any plastic-free wording you use stays accurate.

faqs.q: Can lip packaging board carry recyclable claims after lamination?
faqs.a: A laminate complicates it, because the consumer must separate the film and many recycling streams reject it. Plain or varnished paperboard grades are compatible with standard US curbside paper recycling, so decide disposal positioning before the finish is chosen rather than after artwork.

faqs.q: Is recycled content the same as recyclable for lip carton board?
faqs.a: No. Recycled content and recyclability are different things and are often conflated. We will tell you the recycled share a specific stock carries rather than making a general claim, and recommend understating a claim rather than making one you cannot substantiate.

faqs.q: What board is used for rigid lipstick gift boxes and presentation cases?
faqs.a: Rigid gift boxes and presentation cases use thick rigid board wrapped in printed or specialty paper. They follow different construction rules from flat folding board, with thickness chosen against box size and contents weight, and print quality is as good as the wrap stock allows.

faqs.q: How should I describe my lip product so you can recommend a board?
faqs.a: Describe how the pack is sold and handled, whether shoppers must tell shades apart, what the packed item weighs and whether disposal matters to your positioning. We then recommend a grade and weight with the reasoning, plus a proof on the actual stock before you commit. See the printing options for lip packaging next.

faqs.q: When does digital printing make sense for lip packaging cartons?
faqs.a: Digital printing has almost no setup cost and a flat unit cost, so it suits small runs, many designs in one job, variable data and short lead times. It becomes less economical at high volume, where offset litho's falling unit cost takes over.

faqs.q: At what quantity does offset litho beat digital for lip cartons?
faqs.a: For most lip packaging the crossover falls somewhere between one and three thousand units, moving with the color count and finishing. Ask for pricing at your quantity and the next volume break, since that shows where you sit on the transition.

faqs.q: Should a lipstick shade swatch be printed as a spot Pantone?
faqs.a: Yes. A process build drifts within normal tolerance between runs, and a customer comparing a nude against one bought months ago will notice. A spot Pantone is a pre-mixed ink that reproduces identically, at the cost of an extra ink station.

faqs.q: Where does flexo printing fit for lip balm labels and kraft?
faqs.a: Flexo suits uncoated kraft, simple spot-color work and pressure-sensitive labels. It is less suited to fine gradients and small reverse-out type, so labels with delicate imagery or tiny white text usually belong on another process.

faqs.q: What is ganging and how does it lower lip range printing cost?
faqs.a: Ganging prints several cartons that share a board, ink set and finish on one press sheet, sharing plates, make-ready and press time. A twelve-shade launch printed as one ganged job costs substantially less than twelve separate orders of the same total quantity.

faqs.q: Why do pale colors look metallic on holographic lip gloss boxes?
faqs.a: Metallized and holographic board reflects through translucent process inks, so pale colors come out metallic. Areas that need to read normally require an opaque white layer printed first, set up as its own named layer in the artwork rather than requested at proof.

faqs.q: What is screen printing used for on lip packaging?
faqs.a: Screen printing lays down heavy opaque ink and can be added as a pass at any quantity, which makes it useful for thick white on dark or reflective stock. It is slow as a primary process and unsuited to photographic detail.

faqs.q: Which proof should I approve for lip cartons on kraft or metallized stock?
faqs.a: Ask for a printed proof on the actual stock. A screen proof cannot show how ink sits on kraft or over a reflective base, and colors on kraft shift warmer and darker. Foil and spot UV position and register also need physical checking.

faqs.q: What four figures do you need to quote a lip packaging press?
faqs.a: Total quantity and quantity per design, the number of designs sharing one die line, the color count including spots and any opaque white, and the board grade and weight. With those we quote the press that suits the job and say where an alternative would be cheaper.

faqs.q: Do lip packaging print files differ between digital and litho presses?
faqs.a: No. The file requirements are the same whichever press is used, so artwork does not need rebuilding if a range moves from digital to litho as volumes grow. Full requirements are in the artwork guidelines for print files.

/products/.h2: Questions about our lip packaging products

faqs.q: How many lip packaging formats does Lip Boxes make to order?
faqs.a: Fifteen made-to-order products, grouped by what they hold: lip balm, lipstick, lip gloss and lip care. Each is printed to your artwork and sold online at $30.00 for a pack of 100 ($0.30 each), and larger or custom runs are quoted to your specification.

faqs.q: Which lip balm packaging formats can I choose between?
faqs.a: Lip balm options include folding cartons, coordinated packaging sets, hang tab cartons, printed paper push-up tubes, natural kraft cardboard tubes and wrap labels for tubes, tins and jars. Our lip balm packaging guide and sets compares them side by side.

faqs.q: What lipstick packaging constructions are available from Lip Boxes?
faqs.a: Lipstick packaging comes as printed folding cartons cut to your case, rigid set-up boxes in magnetic, drawer and lift-off lid formats, and hang tab cartons with a euro slot and front window for pharmacy and clip strip display.

faqs.q: Why are lip gloss boxes taller than lipstick or lip balm cartons?
faqs.a: Gloss cartons have to clear a wand applicator, and a doe-foot cap adds height above the reservoir. Slim printed gloss cartons are sized to the assembled height of squeeze tubes, wand applicators and roller balls, which is why they look tall for their volume.

faqs.q: Do you package lip masks and hydrogel lip patches?
faqs.a: Yes. Lip mask cartons cover hydrogel lip patches and lip sleeping masks in single-sachet, multipack and jar formats, with window options where showing the product helps explain it.

faqs.q: Can I package a whole lip care range through one bulk program?
faqs.a: Yes. The bulk and private label route covers a full lip care range, from balm and gloss through to treatment and gift sets. Buying a whole range together is usually cheaper than sourcing each product separately, because board, finish and print runs can be shared.

faqs.q: Are any lip packaging products held in stock for quick dispatch?
faqs.a: No. Nothing is held in stock, because every product is made to a die line drawn for a specific container. That means we cannot ship stock boxes immediately, but the pack fits your product properly when it arrives.

faqs.q: Is there a plastic-free option for lip balm sticks?
faqs.a: Rolled paperboard push-up tubes avoid plastic in the container, supplied kraft or fully printed. Natural kraft cardboard tubes have no bleaching and no plastic component. We confirm the exact liner grade so any plastic-free wording stays accurate.

faqs.q: Which lip packaging products suit peg hook retail display?
faqs.a: Hang tab lip balm boxes and hang tab lipstick boxes are cut with a euro slot or round hole tab for peg hooks in pharmacy, gift, convenience and beauty supply retail. Tab geometry is set against the packed weight of the product.

faqs.q: How do I choose the right lip packaging product for my container?
faqs.a: Describe the container you fill and how it is sold, whether shelf, peg, online, gift or wholesale. We will say which formats work, which do not, and what each would cost at your quantity in a written quote.

/request-a-quote/.h2: Questions about requesting a lip packaging quote

faqs.q: What details should a lip packaging quote request include?
faqs.a: Container dimensions or a sample, quantity, how the product is sold and artwork status are the core details. Any fixed launch date helps too. The more you include, the closer the first reply is to a final price.

faqs.q: Can I leave fields blank on the lip packaging quote form?
faqs.a: Yes. Leave a field blank rather than guessing. If something is missing we ask about it rather than assuming a value that would make the quote misleading, so an incomplete request still gets a useful answer.

faqs.q: What does a written lip packaging quote show?
faqs.a: It gives a written price at your quantity and at the next volume break, so you can see where the saving sits. Shipping is free to the US, UK, Canada and Australia, and the production window is confirmed in writing.

faqs.q: What happens after I accept a lip packaging quote?
faqs.a: Once you confirm, a die line is drawn around your container and a structural sample can be made before anything prints. A color proof on the specified stock follows, and both the die line and proof need written sign-off.

faqs.q: Can I upload artwork or a dieline with my lip packaging quote request?
faqs.a: Yes, the form accepts a file upload. Uploads are validated on the server for type and size before being attached, are not published anywhere and are used only to prepare your quote.

faqs.q: Should I quote by dimensions or post a sample lip container?
faqs.a: Either works, but a physical sample is better. For a tube, give the outside diameter and height with the cap on, and for a lipstick, the width at the widest point with the cap fitted. A posted sample removes most fit risk.

faqs.q: Does the online pack price apply to my lip boxes?
faqs.a: The online price is $30.00 for a pack of 100 ($0.30 each), printed full color to your artwork, with free shipping. For a larger run or a different size, material or finish, your quote states the actual unit price for your job.

faqs.q: How quickly are lip packaging quote requests answered?
faqs.a: Quote requests are answered in the order they arrive, during response hours of Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM to 6:00 PM Eastern Time. Complete details in the first request mean fewer follow-up questions before a price comes back.

faqs.q: Can I request a lip packaging quote with no artwork ready?
faqs.a: Yes. Print-ready, in progress or nothing yet are all workable, and we simply plan the job differently. Say which applies when you send the request so the schedule accounts for artwork supply.

faqs.q: Should my lip packaging quote request mention a launch date?
faqs.a: Yes, if a launch or planogram reset is driving the schedule, say so at the start. It changes which print process and finishing we would recommend, and the turnaround time for custom packaging depends on it.

faqs.q: Which resource helps me size a carton for my lip balm tube?

faqs.q: How do the lip packaging resources differ from the blog?
faqs.a: Resources are the evergreen half: sizing tables, checklists to run before sending a file, and definitions for terms on a quote. The lip packaging blog articles cover ideas, comparisons and things that change.

faqs.q: Is there a resource for checking lip packaging artwork before sending?

faqs.q: Which resource explains dieline line types for lip boxes?

faqs.q: What if a lip packaging resource leaves my question unanswered?
faqs.a: Send your dimensions, quantity and artwork status with the quote request, and put the question in the message. We will answer it directly alongside the written quote.

faqs.q: Which insert suits a lip balm tin or salve jar carton?
faqs.a: Use a die-cut platform rather than a collar. A tin is wide and shallow, so it does not sit in a collar and needs an aperture to drop into. Without one it slides across the carton floor and rattles, which reads as cheap before the box opens.

/resources/custom-packaging-cost-guide/.h2: Custom Packaging Cost Guide: common questions

faqs.q: Which one-time costs appear in a custom lip packaging quote?
faqs.a: One-time costs are the cutting die, printing plates, press make-ready, any foil or emboss tooling and the proofing cycle. They do not change with quantity, which is why they dominate a small order and nearly vanish across a large one.

/resources/lip-balm-box-size-guide/.h2: Lip Balm Box Size Guide: common questions

faqs.q: Why does a paper lip balm tube need more carton clearance?
faqs.a: Paperboard has more surface friction than molded plastic, because kraft grips board in a way plastic does not. A paperboard push-up tube therefore needs slightly more running clearance than a plastic twist-up so it drops in and lifts out of the carton freely.

/resources/lip-gloss-box-size-guide/.h2: Lip Gloss Box Size Guide: common questions

faqs.q: Why does a lip gloss carton use a snap-lock base?
faqs.a: A tall slim gloss carton merchandised standing can open downward when lifted by the top. Moving from a simple tuck flap to a snap-lock base stops that, so mention standing display when you request the die line and the base can be specified accordingly.

/resources/lip-product-packaging-guide/.h2: Lip Product Packaging Guide: common questions

faqs.q: Why lock the primary lip container before designing the carton?
faqs.a: Everything downstream is measured from the container. If a tube supplier changes after a carton is approved and the new tube is slightly wider, the die and printed proof are scrap and the launch slips, so confirm a named supplier and lead time first.

/resources/lipstick-box-size-guide/.h2: Lipstick Box Size Guide: common questions

faqs.q: Should a refillable lipstick carton be sized to the shell or refill?
faqs.a: Size it to the outer shell, not the refill. The shell is what sits in the carton and the insert platform should be shaped to it, so measuring the refill alone produces a carton that cannot close around the assembled case.

faqs.q: Why keep window cut lines on a separate dieline layer?
faqs.a: A merged cut and window layer produces a tool that cuts the window as an outer edge, which scraps the run. Keep every line type, including window cuts, perforations and glue areas, on its own named layer in the dieline file.

faqs.q: Why check the separations preview in a prepress review?
faqs.a: Stepping through each plate shows stray or duplicate spot colors, leftover RGB objects and white set to overprint, which makes type vanish on the proof. It is the highest-value five minutes of a prepress review because these errors are invisible on screen.

/resources/packaging-glossary/.h2: Common questions about packaging glossary terms

faqs.q: What does a die line mean on a lip packaging quote?
faqs.a: A die line is the flat drawing of a carton showing every cut and crease. Your artwork must be built onto it and never rescaled, because the same drawing drives the steel rule die that cuts the board.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a tuck end and a seal end carton?
faqs.a: A tuck end closes with flaps tucked into the carton, while a seal end is glued shut after filling. A seal end needs a sealing machine and is used by automated co-packers, so the choice depends on how your line closes cartons.

faqs.q: What does auto-bottom mean on a lip packaging specification?
faqs.a: An auto-bottom is a pre-glued base that forms as the carton is opened. It is faster to assemble and holds more weight than a tuck base, and a snap-lock base sits between the two.

faqs.q: What does SBS stand for in packaging board terms?
faqs.a: Solid bleached sulfate, a white coated folding boxboard. It is the default for full-color cosmetic cartons because it reproduces closest to proof and holds fine detail and small type.

faqs.q: What does pt mean when a quote lists carton board thickness?
faqs.a: Points measure board thickness in thousandths of an inch, so 18pt board is 0.018 inches thick. It is the usual unit for folding cartons in the US. GSM is a weight per square meter rather than a thickness and is not directly convertible.

faqs.q: What is grain direction in a packaging glossary?
faqs.a: Grain direction is the alignment of fibers in the board sheet. Board folds cleanly along the grain and can crack across it, so grain direction affects how cleanly a carton's creases fold.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CMYK process and a spot color?
faqs.a: CMYK process builds colors from cyan, magenta, yellow and black and drifts slightly between runs. A spot color is a pre-mixed ink, usually a named Pantone, that reproduces identically every run but needs an extra ink station.

faqs.q: What is a euro slot in packaging terminology?
faqs.a: A euro slot is the inverted keyhole cut in a hang tab that lets a carton hang on a peg hook. It is the most widely accepted hanging tab shape for pharmacy and convenience retail fixtures.

faqs.q: What do dust flaps do on a folding lip carton?
faqs.a: Dust flaps are the small flaps either side of a tuck. They close off the corners of the carton so a lip balm stick or lipstick cannot slip out through the gaps when the box is handled or shipped.

faqs.q: What does make-ready mean on a packaging print quote?
faqs.a: Make-ready is the press setup before a run, a one-time cost alongside plates, dies and proofing. Ganged designs share it, and spreading one-time costs across more units is why unit price falls with quantity.

faqs.q: Which sample should I request to check my lip balm tube fit?
faqs.a: Request a plain structural sample, cut and creased from the approved die line in the specified board. It answers whether your container fits with the right clearance, how the carton stands and closes, and whether any insert holds.

faqs.q: When are material swatches useful in a lip packaging project?
faqs.a: Swatches help early, while you are deciding between board grades or considering a specialty stock. They show how board and label stock look and feel, and how holographic film shifts in real light, which no image can show.

faqs.q: Should holographic lip gloss swatches be compared side by side?
faqs.a: Yes. Holographic film behaves very differently under store lighting, daylight and a phone flash, so we recommend rainbow, mirror and pearlescent swatches side by side before committing to holographic lip gloss boxes.

faqs.q: What sample does a rigid lipstick box get before production?
faqs.a: A rigid box gets an assembled white sample instead of a plain cut-and-creased one. Besides fit, it lets you judge proportion, lid fit and magnet strength before the wrapped production run begins.

faqs.q: Should I test a structural lip carton sample empty or filled?
faqs.a: Filled, with your real product. A fit that works on paper can fail with a slightly pillowed sachet, a lacquered lipstick case that measures larger than its drawing, or a paper tube with more friction than a plastic one.

faqs.q: What four checks should I run on a structural lip box sample?
faqs.a: Check the container goes in and out without forcing or rattling, the carton closes cleanly at packing speed, it stands upright with a base that holds when lifted by the top, and any insert keeps the product in place when shaken.

faqs.q: When is a digital proof enough for lip packaging color approval?
faqs.a: A calibrated digital proof is enough on plain coated white board with process color. On kraft, metallized, holographic or black-through stock it is not, because those substrates do not behave like white paper.

faqs.q: Do foil and spot UV lip cartons need a production-standard sample?
faqs.a: Ask for one rather than a flat proof. Position and register on foil, embossing and spot UV need physical checking, and the raised or reflective effect cannot be judged from a printed simulation.

faqs.q: How do I request a lip packaging sample?
faqs.a: Say what you need to verify and send the container if you have one. Use the quote request form and note the sample in the additional details field. Availability, cost and lead time are confirmed in writing for each type.

faqs.q: What can a lip packaging sample not tell me?
faqs.a: A single sample does not show production variation, a digital proof on white does not predict color on another substrate, and no sample verifies regulatory compliance or long-term shelf behavior, such as a soft balm in a paper tube.

faqs.q: What is the standard lead time for custom lip packaging?
faqs.a: Production takes 5–7 business days after you approve the proof, for the online pack and most quoted runs. A run with extra passes, such as litho with foil, spot UV and an insert, gets its own window in writing on the quote.

faqs.q: Which stages of a lip packaging lead time depend on the customer?
faqs.a: Die line approval, artwork supply and proof sign-off sit with you. Production starts at proof approval, so a job where proofs return the same day finishes noticeably sooner than an identical job where they take two weeks.

faqs.q: Which finishes add the most time to lip packaging production?
faqs.a: Lamination adds a converting pass and curing, foil and embossing need a metal die first, spot UV needs a screen or plate and an extra pass, and window patching needs another machine pass. Inserts and rigid construction add further steps.

faqs.q: Does a new paper lip balm tube diameter add lead time?
faqs.a: Yes. Rolled paper tubes are tooled per diameter, so a new diameter adds a tooling step. Once made, that tooling carries across every future order in the same size.

faqs.q: How can I shorten a lip packaging schedule safely?
faqs.a: Post a container sample with the inquiry, build artwork to the die line early, review regulated copy during structural sampling, nominate one proof approver and simplify the finishing. Dropping one pass often saves more time than any expediting.

faqs.q: Is it safe to skip the structural sample to save time?
faqs.a: No. Skipping it saves a few days and risks the entire run, because a fit problem found after production cannot be recovered. Testing the sample promptly with real product is the safer way to save time.

faqs.q: Can rush production be arranged for a lip product launch?
faqs.a: Often, by recommending a print process and finishing that suit the timeline rather than expediting an elaborate specification. A digitally printed carton with varnish turns around considerably faster than a foiled litho job.

faqs.q: What parts of a lip packaging schedule cannot be compressed?
faqs.a: Your approval time and the physical curing of laminates and inks cannot be compressed. Tell us the date early and we will say plainly whether it is achievable and what would have to change.

faqs.q: Is transit time included in the lip packaging production window?
faqs.a: No. A production window ends when the goods leave, not when they arrive. Shipping is free, and delivery takes 5–7 business days in the US and 7–10 to the UK, Canada and Australia, as set out in the shipping and delivery information.

faqs.q: Do multiple lip SKUs take longer than a single carton?
faqs.a: Multiple SKUs mean more artwork to approve and more dies to make, which adds time. Even so, a range produced together is far quicker than placing the same products as sequential orders.
